content_list.content_text: In the 1950s, the old studio system and even the idea that Hollywood was the world center of cinema were toppled. In the following decade, Hollywood - like all of American society - lived through a state of upheaval.

The court-ordered separation of the major studios' production and distribution arms was followed by a proliferation of "runaway productions" - big American productions shot abroad to use box office receipts frozen in countries whose laws required money earned there to be spent there, or to take advantage of resources such as cheaper labor. Even so, the major studios managed to stay afloat as Los Angeles replaced New York as the main center of television production.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Some Like It Hot
information.contentText: The American Film Institute named it the greatest comedy of all time.

content_list.content_text: Judging by the box office and awards lists, one might think little had changed. Big musicals and historical epics dominated the 1960s, although newer genres such as the technically British James Bond series and spaghetti Westerns made their way into the landscape.

The 007 films were born of the same climate of paranoia responsible for American productions such as The Manchurian Candidate (1962). Spaghetti Westerns turned Clint Eastwood (b. 1930) of Rawhide (1951) into a solid Hollywood icon, but their production was 100 percent Italian. Hollywood stayed in the game, even if James Coburn's agent Derek Flint was no match for Sean Connery's unbeatable James Bond. Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) and The Wild Bunch (1969) put a new face on the Italian reinvention of the Western.

information.contentText: At the time, to help with the shoot, Tiffany's opened on a Sunday for the first time in the 20th century.

content_list.content_text: It was also a time of crisis for the old way of doing things. The excesses of Cleopatra (1963) brought Twentieth Century Fox to the brink of bankruptcy and the era of epic cinema to an end. Similarly, films such as Doctor Dolittle (1967) showed that big musicals - in many ways the greatest success story of the 1960s - were not infallible.

quote.quote: Look at that! Look how she moves! That's just like Jell-O on springs
quote.author: Jerry (Jack Lemmon) in Some Like It Hot

content_list.content_text: The idea that a studio should pour most of its resources into one or two blockbusters took several blows during the decade. The veteran executives at Universal and Columbia who saw profits sprouting from films born of the 1960s counterculture, such as Easy Rider (1969), without understanding their appeal, were dethroned in the New Hollywood by younger producers such as Robert Evans, of Paramount.

Still, some points would yet be scored by film industry veterans such as Billy Wilder (1906-2002). His comedy-drama The Apartment (1960) starred his favorite, Jack Lemmon (1925-2001), as a lonely insurance clerk devoted to currying favor with senior managers by lending them his apartment for their extramarital affairs.

information.contentText: The screenplay was written by Walon Green, Roy N. Sickner, and Sam Peckinpah. It is a controversial film because of its stylized violence, with many scenes shot in slow motion. In 1993 and 2006 the film was re-edited, and several extras were added for the DVD, including making-of documentaries. The film's main theme is the end of the Old West and of the cowboy era. The Mexican general appears in a red car instead of on horseback. Among the Mexican army's weapons is a deadly M1917 Browning machine gun, capable of decimating a small army. The gang leader, Pike, uses an M1911 automatic pistol instead of the traditional "six-shooter". Many see a parallel between the film's violence and the Vietnam War, which was in full swing at the time of shooting.

content_list.content_text: Following in the footsteps of the immensely popular Some Like It Hot (1959), The Apartment was a huge commercial success that won five Oscars, including Best Director and Best Picture, even though its treatment of adultery drew disapproval in some quarters.

The new young directors - some coming from television - such as Arthur Penn (1922-2010), Norman Jewison (b. 1926), Mike Nichols (b. 1931), and Sydney Pollack (1934-2008), were open to the influence of the new Europe and of old Hollywood. Blake Edwards (b. 1922) had begun to make his name with his comedies, especially the popular Pink Panther series. He directed Audrey Hepburn (1929-1993) in one of her most important roles, the quirky call girl Holly Golightly in Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961). Sidestepping the seedier aspects of Truman Capote's original, Edwards used his flair for the genre to make it one of the most memorable romantic comedies of the decade.

information.contentText: Four police motorcycles were customized for the film, three of which were stolen before shooting wrapped.

content_list.content_text: In the early 1960s, the lists of movie stars were dominated by performers such as Cary Grant, Elizabeth Taylor, Frank Sinatra, and John Wayne. By the end of the decade, the leading names in the film pantheon were Paul Newman, Warren Beatty, Faye Dunaway, Robert Redford, Dustin Hoffman, Sidney Poitier, Jane Fonda, and Barbra Streisand. And it was not just a matter of youth and beauty: Charles Bronson and Lee Marvin, former supporting tough guys, were elevated to leading roles in action films, while the star of the highest-grossing American film of 1966, Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1966), was Elizabeth Taylor (1932-2011), an old-guard actress.

Adapted from Edward Albee's play, the film, with only four characters, shows Taylor spewing obscenities and Richard Burton (1925-1984) taking all the punishment. The choice of the famous beauty to play the frumpy Martha raised doubts, but her vigorous performance alongside stars such as Burton, George Segal (b. 1934), and Sandy Dennis (1937-1992) ended up being highly praised.

information.contentText: Columbia Pictures agreed to finance the film on the condition that Peter Sellers play at least four major roles in it. The condition reportedly arose from the studio's impression that much of the success of Lolita (1962), Kubrick's previous film, had been due to Sellers's performance, in which his single character assumes several identities. Sellers had also played three roles in the 1959 film The Mouse That Roared. Kubrick accepted the demand, stating that "such crass and grotesque stipulations are the sine qua non of the motion-picture business".

content_list.content_text: In New York, John Cassavetes (1929-1989) - who kept up a film acting career to support his work as a writer - was experimenting freely with experimental cinema, while Andy Warhol (1928-1987) turned his cameras on drug addicts, prostitutes, losers, and drag queens to turn them into "superstars". American directors such as Stanley Kubrick (1928-1999) and Richard Lester (b. 1932) preferred to work in Britain, which had experienced its own New Wave. One of Kubrick's great films of the decade was the black comedy Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964).

quote.quote: I had the privilege of making films at a time when cinema dared to deal with people and their relationships with one another and with society
quote.author: John Schlesinger, Director of Midnight Cowboy

content_list.content_text: In the United States, newcomer filmmakers such as John Schlesinger (1926-2003), John Boorman (b. 1933), and Roman Polanski (b. 1933) cast a fresh eye on the country in vigorous, unsettling films. The elegant revenge thriller Point Blank (1967), directed by John Boorman (b. 1933) and adapted from a pulp fiction classic, starred Lee Marvin (1924-1987), who had asked for the Englishman to take the director's chair.

information.contentText: The film broke several taboos and was a box office and critical hit, very popular with the young generation of the '60s. Influenced by the French New Wave, the film is famous both for its fast-paced editing and for its rapid shifts in narrative tone, moving quickly from humor to the most extreme violence. Controversial upon release for its alleged glorification of killers and its level of on-screen violence, Warner Brothers had so little faith in its box office prospects that it offered Beatty, a first-time producer and the film's great champion, 40% of the gross instead of a producer's usual salary. Six years later, Bonnie and Clyde had already earned $70 million worldwide and turned Warren Beatty into a millionaire.

content_list.content_text: Marvin plays a lone killer who takes on a large, impersonal corporation hidden behind a cloak of respectability. The film's striking scenes and frenetic pace show the influence of the French New Wave. Point Blank proved more interesting to directors than to contemporary audiences, although its reputation has grown steadily ever since.

One of the most powerful films of the late decade, Midnight Cowboy (1969), directed by fellow foreigner Schlesinger, shed light on America's underclass and the taboo of male prostitution. The drama boosted the career of then-unknown actor Jon Voight (b. 1938), popularized Harry Nilsson's melancholy theme song, and won three Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director.

information.contentText: While shooting the scene in which Hoffman and Jon Voight walk through the streets of New York in Midnight Cowboy (1969), a taxi ran through the filming barriers and nearly hit the actors. That's when Dustin lost his temper with the driver and shouted: "Hey, I'm walkin' here!" None of this was in the screenplay.

content_list.content_text: The history of 1960s Hollywood films can also be viewed through the lens of changing censorship standards and sociopolitical attitudes. It was a time of transition between the Rat Pack and Woodstock, between John Kennedy's idealistic Camelot and the fervent mobilizations for civil rights and against the Vietnam War.

The old 1990 Motion Picture Production Code was on its way out, and the new rating system had to take into account the more overt treatment of sex, violence, and profanity. By the end of the decade, "mainstream" films were trying to show and say things that had until then been the exclusive domain of exploitation-film specialists such as Russ Meyer (1922-2004).

At the end of the anything-goes 1960s, Meyer was invited to make a "big picture" at Twentieth Century Fox - Beyond the Valley of the Dolls (1970). The final shootouts of Bonnie and Clyde (1967), by Arthur Penn (1922-2010), and The Wild Bunch (1969), by Sam Peckinpah (1925-1984), are marked by unprecedented levels of violence.

information.contentText: The film became known, among other reasons, for its soundtrack by folk duo Simon & Garfunkel (featuring songs that would become pop hits, such as The Sound of Silence and Mrs. Robinson) and for launching the career of the then-unknown Dustin Hoffman. In addition, some of its scenes became archetypes for many films of a similar genre produced to this day, and have even been parodied many times across various media.

content_list.content_text: The suggestive comedies of Rock Hudson (1925-1985) and Doris Day (1922-2019), which tread carefully on sexual themes, gave way to neurotic, cynical essays on modern mores, very much in the spirit of the times, such as The Graduate (1967). Liberal attitudes were piling up: Spencer Tracy (1900-1960) was forced to accept Sidney Poitier (b. 1927) as a prospective son-in-law in Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967), although Black audiences preferred him demanding respect from Rod Steiger in In the Heat of the Night (1967): Norman Jewison's (b. 1926) film, whose protagonist is an African American detective investigating a murder in a racist small town in Mississippi, reflects the tension of the civil rights era.

quote.quote: This used to be a helluva good country. I can't understand what's gone wrong with it
quote.author: George Hanson (Jack Nicholson) in Easy Rider

content_list.content_text: Thanks to his work in late masterpieces by John Ford (1894-1973) and Howard Hawks (1896-1977), John Wayne remained a box office champion, finally winning an Oscar for True Grit (1969). Clint Eastwood was the cowboy hero of younger audiences, who even liked their police heroes - such as Steve McQueen (1930-1980) in Bullitt (1968) - to be alienated, impassive, and anti-establishment. Directed by another English expatriate, Peter Yates (b. 1929), Bullitt is still famous for its long car chase through the streets of San Francisco, unprecedented in film history, which earned editor Frank P. Keller an Oscar.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Guess Who's Coming to Dinner
information.contentText: The film was one of the few of its time to portray an interracial marriage in a positive light, since interracial marriage had historically been illegal in most U.S. states. It was still illegal in 17 states - mostly Southern states - until June 12, 1967, six months before the film was released.

content_list.content_text: Even in the safest genres, traditionally Oscar winners, the signs of the times could be felt: in the historical film A Man for All Seasons (1966), an anti-authoritarian rebel is crushed by the system, much like the bikers gunned down by truckers in Easy Rider.

Let us not forget that Oliver! (1968) is a tuneful musical about crooks, murderers, pedophiles, and prostitutes comparable to Joe Buck and Ratso Rizzo in Midnight Cowboy (1969). The decade's first Best Picture Oscar winner, The Apartment (1960), deals with disillusionment with the American dream; the last, Midnight Cowboy, is about the lives of outcasts and the marginalized who cannot even aspire to the desperate position of Billy Wilder's corporate parasite.

information.contentTitle: The famous chase scene in Bullitt
information.contentText:
The car chase over the hills of San Francisco, with the vehicles leaping at high speed, is one of the film's most famous scenes. One of the cars was a Dodge Charger R/T, driven by a hitman, while the other was Bullitt's Ford Mustang GT 390.

Its innovative style encouraged and influenced the production of other highly successful crime films in the following years, such as Dirty Harry and The French Connection. And it is often referenced in car chase films, as in the final scene of 2009's Race to Witch Mountain.

content_list.content_text: Times would keep changing. Producer Roger Corman (b. 1926) would soon establish a policy of giving experience and opportunities to young talent, which would allow emerging innovators such as Francis Ford Coppola (b. 1939) and Martin Scorsese (b. 1942) to write and direct their own films. In 1969, barely out of his teens, Steven Spielberg (b. 1946) directed Joan Crawford (1904-1977) in a segment of the pilot for the TV series Night Gallery, while George Lucas (b. 1944) was working on his debut feature, THX 1138.

movies.title: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
movies.original_title: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
movies.overview: After the insane General Jack D. Ripper initiates a nuclear strike on the Soviet Union, a war room full of politicians, generals and a Russian diplomat all frantically try to stop the nuclear strike.

movies.title: Bonnie and Clyde
movies.overview: In the 1930s, bored waitress Bonnie Parker falls in love with an ex-con named Clyde Barrow and together they start a violent crime spree through the country, stealing cars and robbing banks.

movies.title: Some Like It Hot
movies.overview: Two musicians witness a mob hit and struggle to find a way out of the city before they are found by the gangsters. Their only opportunity is to join an all-girl band as they leave on a tour. To make their getaway they must first disguise themselves as women, then keep their identities secret and deal with the problems this brings - such as an attractive bandmate and a very determined suitor.

movies.title: Breakfast at Tiffany's
movies.overview: Fortune hunter Holly Golightly finds herself captivated by aspiring writer Paul Varjak, who's moved into her building on a wealthy woman's dime. As romance blooms between Paul and Holly, Doc Golightly shows up on the scene, revealing Holly's past.

movies.title: The Wild Bunch
movies.overview: Aging outlaw, Pike Bishop prepares to retire after one final robbery. Joined by his gang, Dutch Engstrom and brothers Lyle and Tector Gorch, Bishop discovers the heist is a setup orchestrated in part by a former partner, Deke Thornton. As the remaining gang takes refuge in Mexican territory, Thornton trails them—resulting in fierce gunfights with plenty of casualties.

movies.title: Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?
movies.overview: A bitter, aging couple, with the help of alcohol, use a young couple to fuel anguish and emotional pain towards each other.

movies.title: Midnight Cowboy
movies.overview: Joe Buck is a wide-eyed hustler from Texas hoping to score big with wealthy New York City women; he finds a companion in Enrico "Ratso" Rizzo, an ailing swindler with a bum leg and a quixotic fantasy of escaping to Florida.

movies.title: The Graduate
movies.overview: Benjamin, a recent college graduate very worried about his future, finds himself in a love triangle with an older woman and her daughter.

movies.title: Easy Rider
movies.overview: A cross-country trip to sell drugs puts two hippie bikers on a collision course with small-town prejudices.

movies.title: Guess Who's Coming to Dinner
movies.overview: Matt and Christina Drayton are a couple whose attitudes are challenged when their daughter brings home a fiancé who is black.

movies.title: Bullitt
movies.overview: Senator Walter Chalmers is aiming to take down mob boss Pete Ross with the help of testimony from the criminal's hothead brother Johnny, who is in protective custody in San Francisco under the watch of police lieutenant Frank Bullitt. When a pair of mob hitmen enter the scene, Bullitt follows their trail through a maze of complications and double-crosses. This thriller includes one of the most famous car chases ever filmed.
